about.dates: This report covers your session on Wednesday 7 October 2026 and was prepared on 7 October 2026. If a session is re-analysed, the report is prepared again and carries the new date.
about.footnote: Measured and prepared with PinPoint Studio. Swing images show only the golfer; video stays in the studio.
about.measured: 50 swings with a 7 iron, filmed down-the-line and face-on at high frame rate. Your body positions are read from the video by pose tracking.
about.notChecked: Some things could not be checked on every swing. How fast the club was moving at its peak: our cameras could see it, but not well enough to judge (50 of 50 swings). When your hips turned fastest: the face-on camera cannot time a turn while you are square to it; a down-the-line camera or a body sensor can (31 of 50 swings). When your chest turned fastest: the face-on camera cannot time a turn while you are square to it; a down-the-line camera or a body sensor can (10 of 50 swings). When your hips turned fastest: it was still speeding up when the part of the swing we time had ended (6 of 50 swings). Two more are listed in the technical appendix. Where that touches one of your work-ons, its page says so.
about.ranges: Each habit is judged against a target range. Most ranges are coaching judgement, set from what good ball-strikers do; a few come from published measurements. They are not fitted to you. A swing outside the range is not a mistake in itself — it is where the evidence points. “Ruled out” on a work-on page means measured, and fine, on these swings with these cameras — not gone for good.

workOns.check: Film face-on. At impact your chest should be roughly square to the ball and still turning, with your hips already a little more open than your chest.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Chest peaks after impact.
workOns.cue: Feel your chest turn hard toward the ball as you come down, rather than saving the turn for after it.

drills.instruction: Make swings with a one-second pause at the top. From the pause, start down with your lower body, letting your weight move toward your lead foot while your chest stays behind the ball for a moment. Start with half swings and short irons.
drills.label: Pause at the top
drills.note: The pause is a rehearsal, not a new swing. Once the order feels natural, let the pause shrink until it has gone.
drills.targets: To give your lower body time to start the downswing, so your upper body is not rushed toward the ball.

workOns.goal: Let your chest reach full speed before the ball
workOns.kicker: Work-on 1 of 5  ·  P7, at impact  ·  24 of 50 swings
workOns.name: Chest peaks after impact
workOns.saw: Your chest is still speeding up after the ball — on 24 of 50 swings, no change from first swing to last. Typical when your chest reached full speed: at impact.
workOns.why: A chest still speeding up after the ball has not passed its speed on to your arms and the club in time for the strike.

workOns.check: Film face-on. At impact your belt buckle should already face between the ball and the target, a sign your hips got going early.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Hips peak after impact.
workOns.cue: Start the downswing with your lower body, so your hips are already turning hard by the time your hands reach your trail thigh.

drills.instruction: Start with your feet together, make a backswing, and step toward the target with the lead foot as you start down. Small shots first.
drills.label: Step-through
drills.note: It exaggerates on purpose. The aim is the sequence, not the step.
drills.targets: To feel the weight arriving on the lead side before the club does.

drills.instruction: Make swings with a one-second pause at the top. From the pause, start down with your lower body, letting your weight move toward your lead foot while your chest stays behind the ball for a moment. Start with half swings and short irons.
drills.label: Pause at the top
drills.note: The pause is a rehearsal, not a new swing. Once the order feels natural, let the pause shrink until it has gone.
drills.targets: To give your lower body time to start the downswing, so your upper body is not rushed toward the ball.

workOns.goal: Let your hips reach full speed well before the ball
workOns.kicker: Work-on 2 of 5  ·  P7, at impact  ·  8 of 13 swings
workOns.name: Hips peak after impact
workOns.saw: Your hips are still speeding up after the ball — on 8 of 13 swings, no change from first swing to last. Typical when your hips reached full speed: 7 ms after impact. It could not be measured on 37 of 50 swings: the face-on camera cannot time a turn while you are square to it; a down-the-line camera or a body sensor can.
workOns.why: Hips that are still speeding up after the ball have not handed their speed on to your chest, arms and club in time for the strike.

workOns.check: Film face-on and hold the finish until the ball lands. Your hips should be stacked over your lead foot, and you should be able to stand there without stepping.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Cannot hold the finish, or “falling over”, “stepping through”.

consistency.basisText: σ 12% stance width · 1.19 of corridor · n 50

workOns.cue: Feel yourself swing to a tall finish with your weight on your lead heel and your trail toe just resting on the ground.

drills.instruction: Hit the shot and hold your finish, balanced on the lead foot, until the ball lands. If you cannot hold it, take 20 yards off the swing and try again.
drills.label: Hold the finish
drills.note: The most diagnostic drill in this list: where you fall tells you what happened earlier.
drills.targets: To make balance the constraint the swing is built inside, rather than something checked afterwards.

drills.instruction: Stand with your feet together and hit easy half to three-quarter shots off a low tee. Let your arms swing and your body turn only as fast as you can stay balanced, and hold the finish each time.
drills.label: Feet-together swings
drills.note: Short shots only. If you cannot stay balanced even at half speed, balance on one leg is worth checking before anything else.
drills.targets: To feel the arms, body and club working together at a speed your balance can support, rather than the body lunging or the arms going on their own.

workOns.figureLabel: Each dot is one swing: how far your hips finish from over your lead foot, in percent of stance width.
workOns.goal: Finish balanced over your lead foot
workOns.kicker: Work-on 3 of 5  ·  P10, at the finish  ·  45 of 50 swings
workOns.name: Cannot hold the finish
workOns.saw: You can't hold your finish — on 45 of 50 swings, no change from first swing to last. Typical how far your hips finish from over your lead foot: 55% stance width, against a target of 35% stance width or less; this is a clear miss: well past the range on 38 of 50 swings.
workOns.target: How far your hips finish from over your lead foot: 35% stance width or less, on most swings. Today: 55% stance width.
workOns.why: A finish you can't hold shows your swing was off balance earlier, so your shots are hard to repeat.

workOns.cameWith: The coaching model says it can bring other habits with it. Not today — on every swing we could see, you get the ball up in the air.

workOns.check: Film from down the line. At impact your back and hips should still sit on the lines you drew at address.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Loss of posture, or “loss of posture”, “losing your posture”.
workOns.cue: Feel your chest stay over the ball and your seat stay back until the ball has gone.

drills.equipment: a wall, or the back of a chair
drills.instruction: Stand with your back to a wall and set up so that your backside just touches it, with a club held across your chest. Turn slowly to the top and back down to where impact would be. Your trail back pocket should stay on the wall going back, and your lead back pocket should find it as you turn through, without pushing hard into it or coming away from it.
drills.label: Backside on the wall
drills.note: If your hips can only turn by moving toward the ball, the limit may be in how far your hips can turn, and a physical check comes before more practice.
drills.targets: To feel your hips turn while keeping their distance from the ball, so your arms keep the room they had at address.

drills.instruction: Hold an alignment stick along your spine, touching the back of your head, your upper back and your tailbone. Rehearse your address position and your backswing turn keeping all three in contact.
drills.label: Rod along the spine
drills.note: A fixed upper-back curve will stop all three touching. That is information, not a failure.
drills.targets: To feel the spine angle you set at address being kept through the turn.

workOns.goal: Keep your address posture through the ball
workOns.kicker: Work-on 4 of 5  ·  P7, at impact  ·  49 of 50 swings
workOns.name: Loss of posture
workOns.saw: You stand up out of your posture through impact — on 49 of 50 swings, no change from first swing to last.
workOns.why: Standing up lifts the bottom of your swing, so contact gets thin and harder to repeat.

workOns.also: “leaning left at the top”, “forward spine angle at the top”

workOns.check: Film face-on. At the top your head and chest should sit a little behind the ball, never toward the target.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Reverse spine angle at P4, or “leaning left at the top”, “forward spine angle at the top”.
workOns.cue: At the top, feel your breastbone stay over your trail thigh.

drills.equipment: a mirror, or a phone on a stand
drills.instruction: Without a ball, hold a club across your chest. Turn to the top and check in a mirror, or on a phone face-on, that your head and chest sit a little behind the ball, with your upper body tilted slightly away from the target. Make ten slow turns.
drills.label: Club across the chest
drills.note: A short turn often hides inside this one: if the shoulders cannot turn further, the body tips instead, and a physical check of your upper back comes first.
drills.targets: To feel your upper body staying behind the ball as it turns, rather than tipping toward the target or hanging too far back.

workOns.figureLabel: Each dot is one swing: lean away from the target at the top, in degrees.
workOns.goal: Lean slightly away from the target at the top
workOns.kicker: Work-on 5 of 5  ·  P4, at the top  ·  50 of 50 swings
workOns.name: Reverse spine angle at P4
workOns.saw: You lean toward the target at the top — on all 50 swings, easing as the session went on. Typical lean away from the target at the top: 9° the other way (you lean more toward the target at the top), against a target of 0° or more; this is a clear miss: well past the range on 43 of 50 swings.
workOns.target: Lean away from the target at the top: 0° or more, on most swings. Today: 9° the other way (you lean more toward the target at the top).
workOns.why: Leaning toward the target at the top strains your lower back and makes it hard to start down smoothly.
